text:
Never. Your windows won't sag in any timeframe that matters, including the lifetime of the universe.

Glass at room temperature is an amorphous solid, not a slow liquid. Its viscosity is so high that estimates of how long it would take to flow visibly run far past the age of the universe. Edgar Zanotto's 1998 calculation for medieval cathedral glass put the relaxation time at roughly 10³² years, while the universe is about 10¹⁰ years old.

The thick-bottomed church windows have a different explanation. Before modern float glass (1950s onward), panes were made by spinning molten glass into a disc (crown glass) or blowing and flattening cylinders. Both methods produced sheets of uneven thickness. Glaziers usually set the thicker edge at the bottom because it was more stable, but old windows also turn up with the thick edge at the top or sides, which flow can't explain.

Other evidence points the same way. Roman glassware and ancient obsidian, also a glass, show no sagging after thousands of years. Centuries-old telescope lenses still hold their precise optical figure, which even tiny flow would ruin.

If your house windows ever look wavy or distorted, the cause is the original manufacturing (older glass) or a failed seal in double-glazed units, not flow.
